Case study

HYKR

A Bay Area hiking platform

During my summer internship at BuyMySpot, I wanted to take advantage of the fast-paced startup environment to build something of my own with guidance from my mentor, Ian Herdegen. I spent the last two months designing and developing HYKR, an idea I had for a Bay Area hiking platform.

Tools
Figma, Cursor, Supabase, Vercel
Duration
2 months (May to July 2026)
Contributions
Owned the product from concept to deployment: research, interface design, development, backend, and launch.
Collaborators
Independent project with guidance from Ian Herdegen at BuyMySpot
Problem statement

Not another fitness tracker.

Rather than creating another fitness tracker, I wanted to design an experience where hikers could log adventures, collect peaks, earn XP, and stay motivated to explore the Bay Area.

I noticed that many hiking and fitness apps focused primarily on exercise metrics, while few emphasized exploration and collection. HYKR came from that gap.

Challenge and goals

Own it from concept to launch.

This project allowed me to apply the UX, product design, and AI-assisted development skills I was learning during my internship to a complete product that I owned from concept to deployment.

My goal was to design and launch a functional web application that combined thoughtful user experience with modern development tools. I wanted to create an interface that encouraged exploration while learning new technologies, including Supabase for the backend, Figma for interface design, Cursor for AI-assisted development, and Vercel for deployment.

Research methods

Research first, then design, then build.

I started by researching existing hiking and fitness apps to understand what motivated users to stay engaged. Using those insights, I created the product concept and designed the interface in Figma, establishing the visual identity, typography, color palette, and user flows before writing code.

01

Competitive research

Looked at hiking and fitness apps to see what kept people engaged, and where exploration was missing.

02

Product concept

Defined HYKR around logging adventures, collecting peaks, earning XP, and staying motivated to explore.

03

Interface design in Figma

Set the visual identity, typography, color palette, and user flows before writing code.

04

AI-assisted development

Used Cursor to generate much of the code by writing detailed prompts and refining the output until it matched my design goals.

05

Testing and feedback

Tested the application myself, then refined features, simplified navigation, and improved usability with mentor feedback.

Key findings

Exploration and collection were the opening.

Most apps stop at exercise metrics

I started by researching existing hiking and fitness apps to understand what motivated users to stay engaged. I noticed that many apps focused primarily on exercise metrics, while few emphasized exploration and collection.

Design has to lead the build

Using those insights, I created the product concept and designed the interface in Figma first. Establishing the visual identity and user flows before writing code made it possible to judge whether generated code actually matched the experience I wanted.

Shipping means switching hats constantly

Building HYKR required me to constantly switch between product thinking, UX design, frontend development, backend integration, and troubleshooting deployment issues. That gave me experience across the entire development process.

Design concept

Log adventures. Collect peaks. Earn XP.

Throughout development, I used Cursor to generate much of the application's code by writing detailed prompts and iteratively refining the output until it matched my design goals. I built the backend with Supabase to manage user authentication and hiking data, and deployed the application to Vercel. As I tested the application, I continually refined features, simplified navigation, and improved usability based on my own testing and mentor feedback.

By the end of the internship, I successfully launched a working prototype of HYKR that users could access online. The project significantly strengthened my confidence in rapid product development and taught me how AI can accelerate software development when paired with strong design thinking.

Case study

Laszlo Launchpad

A personal health tech job tracker

I wanted a place to run my health tech job hunt without losing companies, openings, or next steps in a pile of tabs. I built Laszlo Launchpad as a personal system aimed at a summer or fall 2027 start.

Tools
Cursor, Vite, React, TypeScript
Duration
Ongoing personal project, 2026
Contributions
Owned the product from concept to a working app: company atlas, openings, applications, profile, and the weekly scan workflow.
Collaborators
Independent personal project
Walkthrough
Open Launchpad
Problem statement

Not another spreadsheet.

Rather than keeping my hunt in spreadsheets and browser tabs, I wanted one place to watch health tech companies, log openings, and track applications.

I noticed that most job tools are built around a pile of saved postings. They are weaker at helping you stay with a company list over months, especially when you are aiming at UX research, human factors, and product roles in California medtech.

Challenge and goals

Own the hunt until 2027.

This project let me apply product thinking to a problem I actually have. I am targeting summer and fall 2027, so the system has to last, not just hold a weekend of saved jobs.

My goal was a working app I would use every week: a company atlas, an openings list matched to UX research and human factors, an applications pipeline, and a countdown to my start window across SF, San Diego, and LA.

Research methods

Use the hunt as the brief.

I started by mapping how I already hunt: company lists, career pages, LinkedIn saves, and a spreadsheet that went stale. Using those insights, I designed the product around companies first, then openings, then applications. I built the interface in Cursor and kept refining it as I used it.

01

Mapping my hunt

Wrote down where companies, openings, and follow-ups actually lived, and where they fell out of date.

02

Looking at existing trackers

Compared spreadsheets, Notion boards, and saved-job lists. They tracked postings, not a company list over months.

03

Company atlas

Built a list of health tech companies across the Bay Area, San Diego, and LA, with careers pages, stage, and notes.

04

Openings scan

Logged UX research, human factors, and product roles, and kept a Saturday scan so the list did not depend on memory.

05

Using it every week

Opened the app as my actual hunt tool, then simplified navigation and alerts when something was annoying to use.

Key findings

The company is the unit of work.

A posting is easy to forget. A company is not.

A saved job is one moment. A company I care about needs a stage, a careers page, and a last-checked date so I know when to look again. Launchpad is built around that list, not around a pile of tabs.

Career pages go stale fast

If I wait two weeks, I miss the window. The home screen flags companies that need a careers check so the hunt stays current instead of turning back into a spreadsheet I never open.

Not every live role is apply now

Plenty of human factors seats are senior. For a 2027 start, those pages are still useful as networking targets, while the openings list keeps the roles that actually match UX research, human factors, and product.

Design concept

A job system I will actually open.

Home shows the countdown, hunt signals, and the path to 2027. Companies is the atlas. Openings is the matched list. Applications is the pipeline. Profile holds the target cities and roles. Open the walkthrough to click through the real product with sample hunt data.

Home

Countdown to the 2027 start window, what to act on this week, and milestones from now through start.

Companies

The atlas of health tech orgs I want to watch, with stage, priority, and a careers check.

Openings

Roles matched to UX research, human factors, and product, logged from the weekly scan.

Applications

A pipeline for the roles I actually move on, so follow-ups do not live in my inbox.
